title: Impulse and Collision Safety
seo_title: Impulse Worksheets: FΔt = Δp, Air Bags, Helmets and Egg Drops (High School Physics)
standard_text: Apply scientific and engineering ideas to design, evaluate, and refine a device that minimizes the force on a macroscopic object during a collision.
meta_desc: Free high school physics worksheets on impulse and collision safety (NGSS HS-PS2-3): FΔt = Δp, stopping time, bouncing and designing air bags, helmets and egg drops. 100 questions with answers.
key_sub: Impulse FΔt = Δp: safety devices spread the stop over more time.
body_html:
How to think about it

Same change in momentum over a longer time means a smaller force.

  • Impulse J = FΔt = Δp. To stop an object, Δp = mv.
  • Safety devices (air bags, helmets, crumple zones, mats) make Δt longer, so F = Δp ÷ Δt is smaller.
  • Bouncing reverses momentum, so Δp (and the force) is larger than for stopping.
Example

60 kg at 10 m/s stops in 0.5 s. Force?

Δp = 600

600 ÷ 0.5

Answer: 1,200 N

Example

Stop takes 4 times longer. Force?

F = Δp ÷ Δt

Answer: 1/4 as large

Common mistakes

  • Thinking air bags reduce the change in momentum.
  • Thinking a harder surface is safer.
  • Thinking bouncing has a smaller change in momentum.

faq.a: Impulse is force times the time it acts (FΔt). It equals the change in momentum.

faq.q: How do air bags and helmets protect people?
faq.a: They increase the time it takes to stop. With the same change in momentum, a longer time means a smaller force.

faq.q: Why does bouncing cause a larger force?
faq.a: When an object bounces back, its momentum reverses, so the change in momentum is larger than if it just stopped.

items.q: A 2 kg melon moving at 10 m/s is stopped by an average force of 200 N. How long does the stop take?
A 0.5 kg ball moving at 15 m/s stops in 0.25 s. What average force acts on it?
Does an air bag change the passenger's change in momentum?
c: No. It changes the time, which lowers the force.
